questionText:
Read the passage and answer the questions:
 
 The End
of the Civilization
 
There is evidence that by c.1800 BCE most of the Mature Harappan sites in
regions such as Cholistan had been abandoned. Simultaneously, there was
an expansion of the population into new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana
and western Uttar Pradesh. In the few Harappan sites that continued to be
occupied after 1900 BCE there appears to have been a transformation of
material culture, marked by the disappearance of distinctive artefacts of
the civilization—weights, seals, special beads. Writing, long-distance trade
and craft specialization also disappeared. In general, far fewer materials
were used to make far fewer things. Overall, artifacts and settlements
indicate a rural way of life in what are called "Late Harappan" or
"successor cultures".
What brought about these changes? Several explanations have been put
forward. These range from climate change, deforestation, excessive floods,
the shifting and/or drying up of rivers, to overuse of the landscape. Some
of these 'causes' may hold for certain settlements, but they do not explain
the collapse of the entire civilization. It appears that a strong unifying
element, perhaps the Harappan state, came to an end. This is evidenced by
the disappearance of seals, the script, distinctive beads and pottery, the
shift from a standardized weight system to the use of local weights, the
decline and abandonment of cities. The subcontinent would have to wait
for over a millennium for new cities to develop in a completely different
region.
The transformation of what led to occupation of few Harappan sites after
1900 BCE?

questionText:
Read the following excerpt carefully and answer the question that follows:

"Although Harappa was the first site to be discovered, it was badly destroyed by brick-robbers. As early as 1875, Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), often called the father of Indian archaeology, noted that the amount of brick taken from the ancient site was enough to lay brick for 'about 100 miles' of the railway line between Lahore and Multan. Many of the ancient structures at the site were damaged. In contrast, Mohenjodaro was far better preserved. Cunningham, when excavating, found an ancient seal that was given to him. He tried to place it within the time-frame of the sixth century BCE to fourth century CE, the period of the earliest cities he was familiar with from Chinese pilgrim accounts, and thus missed the true antiquity of the Indus Valley."

What critical chronological error did Alexander Cunningham make when attempting to date Harappan artefacts?

options.text: He dated them to the European Middle Ages

options.text: He tried to fit Harappan seals within the time-frame of early historic cities (6th c. BCE to 4th c. CE) known from Chinese pilgrim chronicles

options.text: He considered them to be modern forgeries made by railway workers
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Applies an adjacent or reciprocal mathematical relation.

options.text: He believed they were manufactured in 18th-century Bengal
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Confuses related NCERT concepts or attributes.

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
1. Cunningham relied on records of Chinese Buddhist pilgrims (Faxian and Xuanzang) and assumed Indian urbanization began in the 6th century BCE, missing Harappa's 3rd millennium BCE antiquity.
Hence Option A is correct.
Hence, option (B) is correct.
